questions.text: Two people, P and Q, decide to independently roll two identical dice, each with 6 faces, numbered 1 to 6. The person with the lower number wins. In case of a tie, they roll the dice repeatedly until there is no tie. Define a trial as a throw of the dice by P and Q. Assume that all 6 numbers on each dice are equi-probable and that all trials are independent. The probability (rounded to 3 decimal places) that one of them wins on the third trial is
questions.solution:
A trial ties with probability [latex]\frac{6}{36}=\frac16[/latex]. Someone wins on the 3rd trial if the first two tie and the third does not:
[latex]\left(\frac16\right)^2\times\frac56=\frac{5}{216}\approx0.023[/latex]

Answer: 0.023

questions.text: The time complexity of computing the transitive closure of a binary relation on a set of [latex]n[/latex] elements is known to be
questions.solution:
Warshall's algorithm computes the transitive closure of a relation on n elements with three nested loops: [latex]O(n^3)[/latex].

Answer: [latex]O(n^3)[/latex]

questions.text: Which one of the following Boolean expressions is NOT a tautology?
questions.solution:
Find a falsifying assignment for option 2: a = c = 0 and b = 0. Then [latex]a\leftrightarrow c[/latex] is true, [latex]\sim b[/latex] is true, but [latex]a\wedge c[/latex] is false, so the whole implication is false. Not a tautology.

Options 1 (hypothetical syllogism), 3 and 4 are always true.

Answer: Option 2

questions.text: The symmetric difference of sets A={1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8} and B={1,3,5,6,7,8,9} is:
questions.solution:
Symmetric difference = elements in exactly one set: [latex](A-B)\cup(B-A)=\{2,4\}\cup\{9\}=\{2,4,9\}[/latex].

Answer: {2,4,9}
